newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: FOCUS - Novartis posts strong Q1, but cautions.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Novartis posts strong Q1, but cautions.

text.p: Swiss drugs giant Novartis AG said its 1997 first quarter sales rose by a better than expected 22 percent, but cautioned that growth might not be quite so strong throughout the entire year.
Novartis said in its first quarter report on Thursday that business was particularly strong in pharmaceuticals, thanks to a good start in the key U.S. market.
The Swiss group reported sales of 8.176 billion Swiss francs ($5.6 billion) as compared to 6.683 billion in the comparable 1996 period.
Sales in pharmaceuticals, its largest single business segment, totalled 3.389 billion, representing an increase of 30 percent in Swiss francs and 14 percent in local currencies.
"The sales growth of 14 percent in the pharmaceuticals sector was driven by the performance in the U.S. where sales in the previous year were comparably low," Novartis said.
"This is strong growth when compared to worldwide (industry) growth of seven to eight percent," said Gerd Ramsperger, head of brokerage research at Zuercher Kantonalbank.

Bank Julius Baer analyst Beat Alpiger, who cautioned on Wednesday that the comparisons would be difficult, had been expecting an overall sales rise for the group of 17 percent in Swiss francs and five percent in local currencies.
"The figures were excellent, really better than expected," said one Geneva trader. His bank had expected only an eight percent local currency pharmaceuticals sales increase.
Novartis shares were 37 francs higher at midday, trading at 1,817.
Novartis was officially formed at the start of the year through the merger Ciba-Geigy AG CIGZn.S and Sandoz AG SANZ.S.
The company said today that it had restated 1996 figures for comparison purposes and accordingly, the prior-year figures do not include divested business activities.
The biggest divestiture was the spin-off last month of Ciba Specialty Chemicals, a company that accounted for some 6.7 billion francs in sales during 1996.
Novartis also reiterated its optimistism about the prospects for all of 1997. But it added growth was not likely to remain at these relatively lofty levels for the rest of the year.

Last month when the company reported 1996 results it said the combination of a strong positive currency effect, together with the realisation of merger synergies, should lead to marked improvement in operating and net income in 1997.

"We are very confident about the entire year, that means we see strong growth rates. But I have to say that I would not expect that we would see exceptionally high figures throughout the year," Novartis chief financial officer Raymund Breu said in a telephone interview.

Group sales for the first quarter were eight percent higher when computed in local currencies. Novartis said the 22 percent Swiss franc sales increase was due to the strong positive currency effect. The Swiss franc has weakened substantially against most other major currencies since early 1996.

Key worldwide contributors in the pharmaceuticals sector were the lipid-lowering agent Lescol, which had local currency sales growth of 94 percent, fungal agent Lamisil, which grew by 92 percent, osteoporosis drug Miacalcic with 45 percent growth.
Novartis' agribusiness sales were 17 percent higher, or four percent higher on a local currency basis.
Nutrition division sales rose by 18 percent in Swiss francs and by three percent in local currencies.

But sales in the Animal Health segment fell by eight percent in Swiss francs and by 22 percent in local currencies and Breu said the decline was due to an inventory reduction process at the distributor level taking place in the U.S. since last year.
High inventories were being reduced in the group's Program dog flea control product, he said.
Consumer demand for the product had not declined, but ex-factory sales were down as a result of the inventory reduction, Breu added.
